name: Climbazole

lead: Climbazole is an azole antifungal added to over-the-counter dandruff shampoos, lotions and conditioners, sometimes alongside zinc pyrithione, to cut visible flaking and itching for a cleaner scalp. It targets the Malassezia yeasts thought to contribute to dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.

It belongs to the same class as ketoconazole and is described as inhibiting the fungal enzyme CYP51, which blocks ergosterol production in fungal membranes. Most published research concerns its presence in wastewater, rivers and fish. A 2001 clinical study of a climbazole shampoo for seborrheic scalp eczema is cited by Wikipedia, though no trial details were available.

paras: People use it as part of a regular anti-dandruff shampoo or conditioner routine, left on the scalp briefly before rinsing. It is bought over the counter, often as one active among several.

Local irritation such as redness and itching is reported. Grokipedia describes cosmetic-use limits in the EU and a 2024 ECHA flag for possible endocrine-disrupting properties; it is also reported as toxic to aquatic life.

angle.text: Climbazole is an antifungal in anti-dandruff products that goes after the yeast behind scalp flaking, so hair and shoulders look cleaner. It is in the same azole class as ketoconazole; the research in the sources is mostly environmental.

lead: Climbazole is a synthetic imidazole antifungal used as an active ingredient in over-the-counter anti-dandruff shampoos, lotions and conditioners, and sometimes as a preservative.[1][2] It belongs to the same azole class as ketoconazole, clotrimazole and miconazole and is active against Malassezia yeasts thought to contribute to dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.[1][2]

People use climbazole-containing shampoos to reduce visible flaking and itch so that the scalp, hair and shoulders look cleaner. It also appears in some skincare research as a companion to retinoids: a 2017 study reported that it boosted retinoid-associated activity in skin, and a 16-week trial of a retinyl propionate and climbazole combination examined its effect on the appearance of hyperpigmentation and deep wrinkles.[3][4]

Published trials include shampoo comparisons against zinc pyrithione, a spray study in pityriasis versicolor and a veterinary trial in dogs; a large share of other published work concerns its detection and fate in the environment, including wastewater, rivers and fish.[5][6][7][8][9][10][11]

paras: Climbazole is found in non-prescription shampoos for dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, sometimes combined with zinc pyrithione or triclosan.[1] Grokipedia reports typical cosmetic concentrations of up to 2 percent in rinse-off products and 0.5 percent in leave-on products, where it may serve as both an antidandruff active and a preservative.[2]

Beyond shampoos, a topical spray combining hydroxypropyl chitosan, climbazole and piroctone olamine has been studied in pityriasis versicolor, a Malassezia-related skin condition that causes patchy discoloration.[7] Climbazole is also used in veterinary shampoos, where a 2% product has been tested against Malassezia on dogs.[8]

sections.h: Dandruff, Malassezia and how it is used
paras: Wikipedia describes climbazole as a topical antifungal used for dandruff, seborrhoeic dermatitis and eczema, with high in vitro and in vivo activity against Malassezia species, which are thought to play a role in dandruff.[1] It is often paired with zinc pyrithione or triclosan in over-the-counter shampoos and lotions.[1] Home-use trials of shampoos combining it with piroctone olamine or zinc pyrithione measure visible flaking and scalp condition, which is the appearance outcome users care about.[5][6]

For appearance, climbazole matters mainly through the scalp. Dandruff is a chronic, relapsing scalp condition marked by scaling and itching, and flakes on dark clothing or visible on the hairline are the feature people most often want gone.[1][5] Wikipedia describes climbazole as active against Malassezia yeasts, which are thought to contribute to dandruff, so a shampoo that lowers their numbers is meant to reduce flaking and the itch-scratch cycle that irritates the scalp.[1] A cleaner, calmer scalp is the route by which it supports a tidier-looking head of hair; climbazole itself is not described as acting on hair growth or hair thickness.

A second appearance use is in leave-on skincare research. A 2017 study reported that climbazole at 0.5 percent increased retinoid-associated biological activity when paired with retinol or retinyl propionate, and a 16-week split-face trial reported improved hyperpigmentation and deep wrinkling with minimal irritation for a retinyl propionate and climbazole combination compared with 0.1% retinol.[3][4] In that framing climbazole is a booster for a gentler retinoid, a different role from its antifungal one.

Like other azoles, climbazole is described as inhibiting fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), disrupting synthesis of ergosterol, a key component of fungal cell membranes.[2] Reported minimum inhibitory concentrations against Malassezia species are low, and skin permeation is described as under 1 percent of the applied dose.[2]

Climbazole is 1-(4-chlorophenoxy)-1-(1H-imidazol-1-yl)-3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one, with formula C15H17ClN2O2 and molecular weight about 292.8 g/mol. Grokipedia describes a white to pale-brown crystalline powder that is poorly soluble in water and soluble in ethanol and oils, with a melting point near 97 degrees Celsius.[2]

Wikipedia notes that climbazole may cause local irritation such as redness, rash and itching.[1] Grokipedia reports negative mutagenicity tests and that EU regulators classified it as acceptable for cosmetic use within limits, while a 2024 ECHA assessment flagged potential endocrine-disrupting properties in the environment with human relevance still under evaluation; this account is AI-generated and should be treated cautiously.[2]

Environmental research has detected climbazole among personal-care product residues in wastewater and surface waters, and an ecotoxicity study examined its effects on aquatic organisms.[12][13][14][15] Studies in grass carp reported liver cell apoptosis and lipid accumulation and oxidative stress and inflammation in the gut after exposure to micrograms-per-litre concentrations.[16][17]

Percutaneous absorption has been examined directly: a 2025 in vitro study measured how much climbazole passes through human skin, and a 2022 review discussed how surface concentration affects skin penetration across topical chemicals generally.[9][18] Environmental findings, including detection in wastewater and in wild fish in Chinese rivers, are discussed in the literature on personal-care biocides rather than in studies of scalp performance.[13][14][15]

A 2011 randomized comparison in subjects with moderate to severe dandruff tested a shampoo with 0.5% piroctone olamine and 0.45% climbazole against a commercial 1% zinc pyrithione shampoo, with in vitro antimycotic work, a pig-skin substantivity model and home-in-use studies.[5]

The 2013 randomised, double-blind trial enrolled 620 men and women and used scalp flaking and epidermal histamine level as endpoints. Its authors reported that the shampoo with maximised zinc pyrithione bioavailability showed greater antifungal potency in the laboratory than the dual-active shampoo containing zinc pyrithione and climbazole, and the study was framed as a comparison of two strategies for improving antifungal shampoos: raising delivery of one active versus adding a second.[6] The 2011 comparison of 0.5% piroctone olamine plus 0.45% climbazole against 1% zinc pyrithione reported comparable antifungal effectiveness in vitro, higher substantivity on pig skin for the piroctone olamine and climbazole shampoo, and improvements in scalp condition and itching in home-use subjects, with wet combing force also assessed as a cosmetic outcome.[5]

A 2013 randomized clinical trial compared a potentiated zinc pyrithione shampoo with a zinc pyrithione and climbazole shampoo, assessing antifungal potency in vitro and delivery of zinc pyrithione particles in the follicular infundibulum.[6] In a 2017 multicenter study, 30 patients with pityriasis versicolor (average age 20.8 years) used the chitosan, climbazole and piroctone olamine spray twice weekly rather than daily, with confocal microscopy used to examine persistence in the stratum corneum.[7]

For skin appearance, a 2017 study combined cell culture, skin-equivalent models and a clinical test on the forearms of 16 subjects (climbazole at 0.5% with retinol or retinyl propionate) and reported that climbazole boosted retinoid-associated biological activity.[3] A 16-week randomized, double-blind, split-face trial of 45 women aged 40 to 70 with moderately photodamaged skin compared retinyl propionate plus climbazole with 0.1% retinol and, per its title, reported improvement in the appearance of hyperpigmentation and deep wrinkling with minimal irritation.[4]

In 11 beagles with naturally occurring Malassezia, a 2% climbazole shampoo applied weekly for two weeks was compared with a shampoo base in a 2015 randomized trial.[8] A 2025 in vitro study measured percutaneous absorption of climbazole through human skin, and a 2024 paper described the development of topical formulations.[9][10] Laboratory screening found it among compounds that inhibit exosome release by prostate cancer cells, which is not a clinical use.[11]

Climbazole is rarely a destination ingredient. People meet it on the back of a dandruff shampoo, often alongside piroctone olamine or zinc pyrithione, and its use is part of the wider conversation about which antifungal active suits a given scalp. It is also used in pet-care products; a 2015 trial applied a 2% climbazole shampoo weekly for two weeks to naturally infected dogs and reported a rapid reduction in Malassezia counts, with the effect still evident after 15 days.[8] In the laboratory, a 2018 high-throughput screen of 4,580 compounds identified climbazole among molecules that modulate exosome release in prostate cancer cells, a finding that sits entirely outside its cosmetic use.[11]
